issues.issue: The recital of the Trust's purpose — a "continuous source of managed investment for cash collateral" for securities lenders — is argued to control the far broader operative investment latitude granted in the Portfolio Diversification list (c031) and the authority to place all assets in another series (c044). Whether this stated purpose limits those operative powers is a live construction question.

The offer is described as made "to qualified institutional purchasers," which does not square with the cover legend's "qualified institutional or accredited investors" or with the "qualified purchasers" of Section 3(c)(7) relied on in c055 and the Subscription Agreement's accredited-investor/qualified-purchaser representations. Which eligibility standard governs admission is left unresolved.

Shareholders become entitled to share in income and gains "upon acceptance of their subscriptions ... and payment of the consideration specified by Wells Fargo from time to time," which cannot be squared with the fixed $10.00 initial price in c007 or with Declaration of Trust Section 4.5 crediting investments at the Net Asset Value next determined. The price at which subscriptions are taken is therefore indeterminate.

Wells Fargo's self-appointment as investment manager, with power to retain affiliated advisers, sits against Declaration of Trust Section 6.1, which bars any contract retaining the Trustee or its affiliates for additional services for additional compensation beyond that disclosed and agreed in the securities lending agreements. Whether the self-appointment is permitted, and on what compensation, must be construed across the two documents.

"The specific portion advised by any of these investment advisers will vary from time to time in the sole discretion of Wells Fargo" supplies no standard, notice or limit on delegation. The provision is standardless as to how much of the portfolio may be handed to a sub-adviser.

Each Share is said to represent "an undivided proportionate interest in all assets and liabilities of the CI Term Trust," whereas Declaration of Trust Section 4.6 makes each Share an equal undivided interest in the net assets of the Series "except to the extent affected by expense allocations." The unqualified statement here and the qualified one there cannot both be given full effect.

Shares are offered "at the then applicable value per Share (as defined below)," but no definition of "value per Share" appears anywhere below in the Memorandum. The cross-reference is broken, leaving the purchase price term undefined.

The minimum initial investment is "determined by Wells Fargo in the efficient management of the securities lending and investment program" — a garbled phrase supplying no ascertainable standard or amount. "Efficient management" has no measurable content as a criterion for a minimum subscription.

Valuing assets "each Business Day at their then current market value" cannot be squared with c029's objective of maintaining a stable $10.00 price per Share, which presupposes amortized-cost valuation, nor with Declaration of Trust Section 5.3's Net Asset Value determined "in a manner consistent with the 1940 Act." Which valuation basis governs redemptions and subscriptions is unresolved.

The mandatory daily declaration and monthly payment of dividends conflicts with Declaration of Trust Section 5.1, which leaves the amount, timing and form of any distribution wholly to the Trustee's discretion. Whether Shareholders have an enforceable entitlement to a daily dividend turns on which text controls.

The enumerated expense list borne by the CI Term Trust is materially narrower than Article Seven of the Declaration of Trust, which charges the Series with legal, compliance, litigation, insurance, printing and Trustee expenses and gives the Trustee a lien. Which expense catalogue governs a disputed charge is left open.

Permitting Wells Fargo and its affiliates to take fees "in amounts that are determined to be reasonable by the Trustee" cannot be squared with Declaration of Trust Section 6.1, which forbids retention of the Trustee or its affiliates for additional compensation beyond that disclosed and agreed in the securities lending agreements, or with the Securities Lending Agreement's fixed 40%/60% split of net earnings. The permissible compensation of the Trustee is therefore in doubt.

Outside-vendor accounting fees "as negotiated by Wells Fargo" are not stated to be within the fees that c014 requires to be "disclosed to Shareholders at least annually." Whether these charges fall inside or outside the annual disclosure duty is unresolved between the two paragraphs.

Permission to use affiliated brokers and broker-dealers "subject to any applicable law" sits against the closing paragraph of Declaration of Trust Section 3.1, which covenants that the Trustee will cause the Trust to comply with the affiliated-transaction prohibitions of Sections 17(a), (d) and (e) of the 1940 Act as if the Trust were registered. Whether affiliated brokerage is permitted at all requires reading the two together.

The flat statement that Shares "may not be transferred or assigned" conflicts with the Declaration of Trust's definition of Shares as "equal proportionate transferable units of interest" and with Section 4.7(b) empowering the Trustee to make rules governing the transfer of Shares. The absoluteness of the bar is therefore contestable.

The redemption right is stated to arise "upon notice to Wells Fargo of at least seven (7) business days ... but no less often than as of the close of each Business Day," two requirements that cannot both operate. Whether a Shareholder may redeem daily or only after a week's notice is unclear on the face of the sentence.

Redemption "at a redemption price equal to the valuation per Share as determined by Wells Fargo" cannot be squared with Declaration of Trust Section 5.2, which fixes the price at Net Asset Value next determined after receipt of the redemption request. Which pricing rule binds the Trustee is left open.

The reservation to postpone payment or suspend redemptions "in certain circumstances as specified in the Declaration of Trust" does not match Declaration of Trust Sections 5.2 and 5.4, which cap suspension at seven days and permit payment wholly or partly in securities. The scope and duration of the suspension power can only be determined by construing the two together.

The exculpation carve-out for "negligence" conflicts directly with Declaration of Trust Section 8.1, which exculpates Covered Persons except for "bad faith, gross negligence, willful misconduct or reckless disregard." Whether simple negligence exposes Wells Fargo to liability depends on which standard controls.

Indemnity conditioned on the absence of the indemnitee's own "negligence" cannot be squared with Declaration of Trust Section 8.2, which mandates indemnification "to the fullest extent permitted under the Maryland Act" subject only to Section 8.1's gross-negligence exception. The scope of the Trust's indemnity obligation is therefore contested between the documents.

Shareholders are promised "the same limitation of liability extended to stockholders of a business corporation," whereas Declaration of Trust Section 4.10 measures it by stockholders of "a private corporation for profit organized under the General Corporation Law of the State of Maryland." The benchmark for shareholder limited liability differs between the two instruments.

Indemnification of Shareholders "from the assets of the Trust" conflicts with Declaration of Trust Section 8.3, which limits the indemnity to "the assets belonging to the applicable Series," and with Section 4.6(b)'s bar on enforcing one Series' obligations against another. Whether Trust-wide assets stand behind this indemnity is unresolved.

The statement that the Declaration "may be amended by the Trustee at any time without Shareholder approval" omits the proviso in Declaration of Trust Section 9.7 that "Shareholders shall have the right to vote on any amendment submitted to them by the Trustee in its discretion." Whether any Shareholder voice on amendments survives depends on reading the two together.

The assurance that "investment decisions for the CI Term Trust are made independently from those other accounts managed by Wells Fargo" cannot be squared with c044's authority to place some, a significant portion or all of the Series' assets in another Wells Fargo series, or with c016's affiliated-brokerage permission. Whether independence is a representation or is disclaimed by those provisions is a construction question.

KPMG is described as "independent auditors for the Trust and Wells Fargo" serving "at the sole discretion of Wells Fargo," while c059 has the same firm giving tax opinions for the Trust. Whether the represented independence is consistent with those dual engagements is nameable but marginal.

"It has no material performance history" uses a materiality qualifier that leaves unclear whether performance of the Trust's other, related series (in which under c044 this Series may invest all of its assets) must be disclosed. The word "material" has no defined boundary here.

The stated objective — safety of principal and "daily liquidity requirements" — cannot be squared with c040's five-year maximum security maturity, c037's 190-day weighted average maturity and c033's 15% allowance for illiquid securities. Whether the objective constrains those permissions, or merely aspires, is the central construction question.

"Will endeavor to maintain a stable $10.00 price per Share" coupled with an immediate disclaimer leaves it unclear whether any obligation at all is undertaken, and "endeavor" has no defined content. The sentence promises and disclaims the same thing.

The quality limit — only obligations "rated in the highest short-term rating category" or unrated equivalents — cannot be squared with c031's authorization to buy mortgage-backed, asset-backed and corporate notes, bonds and debentures, or with c040's five-year maximum maturity, instruments that ordinarily carry long-term rather than short-term ratings. Which restriction governs such purchases is unresolved.

The authorized-investment list (mortgage-backed and asset-backed securities, Rule 144A securities, units of business trusts, corporate bonds and debentures) is far broader than the cash-collateral investments permitted by Section 2(f) of the Securities Lending Agreement, which confines investment to enumerated "short term money market instruments" and mutual funds holding them. Which list governs the reinvestment of a lender's cash collateral must be construed.

"Approved money market funds" and "assets of the Fund" use undefined terms — nothing states who approves, or what "the Fund" is in a document whose defined vehicle is the "CI Term Trust." The eligibility criterion and the subject of the sentence are both left undefined.

The exception to the 5% single-issuer limit for "business trusts that are 2a-7 compliant or 2a-7-like" turns on the term "2a-7-like," which has no ascertainable boundary. Whether a given pooled vehicle qualifies is therefore indeterminate.

Private placements "will generally be considered illiquid unless at least two broker/dealers provide an active secondary market" — "generally" and "active secondary market" leave the classification of a security as illiquid without a workable test. The 15% cap can therefore be measured in more than one way.

The 25% cap on any "industry or sector" is immediately excepted for "the financial services or banking industry," which "may exceed 25%" without any stated ceiling, so the exception can swallow the rule. "Industry or sector" is itself undefined.

"Will review the portfolio and may consider adopting guidelines ... as it deems appropriate in its discretion" imposes no obligation capable of breach and no standard for the review. Whether any duty is created by the sentence is unclear on its own words.

This deferral of the diversification requirements runs to six months after inception or $100 million in assets, "whichever is later," while the identically framed deferral of the maturity requirement in c039 says "whichever is earlier." The two parallel provisions cannot both reflect the intended trigger, and which controls is a question of construction.

A 190-day maximum dollar-weighted average maturity is hard to square with c028's "daily liquidity requirements" objective and c029's stable $10.00 share price, both of which the Memorandum elsewhere ties to Rule 2a-7 concepts with much shorter maturity limits. Whether the 190-day figure or the liquidity/stability objective governs portfolio construction is unresolved.

The general rule deems maturity "the shortest of" stated maturity, next rate reset or next put date, but the following "However" sentence deems a variable rate demand obligation's maturity the shorter of the next rate readjustment or the date the principal can be recovered on demand — the two can yield different dates for the same instrument. Which governs a variable rate demand obligation is not stated.

The weighted average maturity requirement is deferred until six months after inception or $100 million in assets, "whichever is earlier," which is the opposite tie-breaker from the identically worded diversification deferral in c036 ("whichever is later"). The mismatch makes the two deferral periods diverge for no stated reason and invites the argument that one is a drafting error.

A five-year maximum maturity for individual securities cannot be squared with c028's safety-and-daily-liquidity objective or with the Securities Lending Agreement's confinement of cash collateral to short-term money market instruments. Whether five-year paper may be bought for a cash collateral pool is the resulting question.

"For securities using a weighted average life for the maximum maturity determinant, the industry convention for these types of securities will be used" leaves the maturity of amortizing securities to an unidentified "industry convention." No source or definition is supplied for that convention.
